<h3>Block Public Access: do public ACLs and bucket policies count?</h3>
<p>The left side of the embed below holds the switches: Object Ownership (a three-way choice, one option of which disables ACLs), the four Block Public Access switches, and how <code>q3.pdf</code> was encrypted when uploaded, with the KMS key policy below that. The right side holds the bucket policy JSON and <code>q3.pdf</code>'s object ACL. Statements can be added to or removed from the bucket policy and the KMS key policy; the KMS key policy's statements appear after you open "2 statements". The object ACL is shown as is.</p>
<ul>
<li>Set Object Ownership to Bucket owner enforced, which disables ACLs, and <code>q3.pdf</code>'s object ACL and the <code>BlockPublicAcls</code> and <code>IgnorePublicAcls</code> switches turn grey, because S3 no longer counts ACLs when checking access.</li>
<li>The four lines at the top right are the results. Their text never changes; only the colour gives the answer: normal ink means yes, faded means no.</li>
</ul>
<iframe src="/embeds/s3-access-tree" width="100%" height="1084" style="border:0;display:block;margin:1.5rem 0 2.5rem" loading="lazy" title="S3 bucket settings tree: what decides whether q3.pdf can be read"></iframe>
<p>Block Public Access isn't a single switch but a set of four. Each can be on or off on its own; the <a href="https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/access-control-block-public-access.html">S3 Block Public Access page</a> says "These settings are independent and can be used in any combination." They deal with <em>public</em> ACLs and bucket policies. A public ACL is a grant to <code>AllUsers</code> like the one above; a public bucket policy is one like the <code>Principal: "*"</code> statement in the embed, with no limiting <code>Condition</code>, so anyone can read.</p>
<p>In the console's wording, two of the four act on <em>new</em> ones and two on <em>any</em>:</p>
<ul>
<li><code>BlockPublicAcls</code>, <code>BlockPublicPolicy</code> (<em>new</em>): S3 rejects any attempt to write a public ACL or bucket policy. Existing ones are untouched; <code>q3.pdf</code>'s ACL stays in force.</li>
<li><code>IgnorePublicAcls</code>, <code>RestrictPublicBuckets</code> (<em>any</em>): existing ones aren't deleted, but stop working for outsiders. A public ACL doesn't count, so anonymous requests can't read <code>q3.pdf</code>; a public bucket policy works only for users in the bucket owner's account and AWS services. <code>Reader</code> still reads through policies in its own account.</li>
</ul>
<p>If the account, organization or an access point also sets these switches, S3 compares them one switch at a time: a switch on in any of those places counts as on for <code>reports</code>. If the account has <code>IgnorePublicAcls</code> on, public ACLs in <code>reports</code> don't count even though the bucket itself has it off. The organization is the exception: the <a href="https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/access-control-block-public-access.html">Block Public Access page</a> says that at the organization level all four settings apply together, and you can't turn on just one.</p>
<h3>The 2023 defaults</h3>
<p><a href="https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/heads-up-amazon-s3-security-changes-are-coming-in-april-of-2023/">Since April 2023</a>, new buckets have all four on and <a href="https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/about-object-ownership.html">ACLs disabled</a> ("Bucket owner enforced"). With ACLs disabled:</p>
<ul>
<li>the <code>--acl public-read</code> upload above fails with a 400 <code>AccessControlListNotSupported</code>;</li>
<li>existing ACLs no longer take part in access evaluation; the <code>ACL</code> term in the expression is never true, and only the policies decide.</li>
</ul>
<h2>The takeaway</h2>
<p>Next time AWS hands you a new "X policy," ask two questions:</p>
<ol>
<li><strong>Does it name a who, with <code>Principal</code> or <code>NotPrincipal</code>?</strong> If yes, it sits on a resource; if no, on an identity. SCP and RCP are the exception: they attach to an Organizations root, OU or account.</li>
<li><strong>Does it grant access, or only cap it?</strong> If the docs say it does "not grant permissions," it only caps.</li>
</ol>
<p>Then find its cell in the table above. For a KMS key, the key policy must first allow the key's account to use identity-based policies before any identity-based policy takes effect.</p>15:T733e,
AWS keeps inventing policies. S3 bucket policy, SQS queue policy, SNS topic policy, Lambda function policy, KMS key policy, API Gateway resource policy, IAM role trust policy. It looks like a dozen things to learn.

It's one JSON shape, and two questions sort most of them.

## The basic shape

Every one of them is this JSON (the comments are for reading; real policy JSON has none):

```jsonc
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",            // or Deny
    "Principal": { },             // who
    "Action": ["s3:GetObject"],   // what they may do
    "Resource": "arn:...",        // on which thing
    "Condition": { }              // when (optional)
  }]
}
```

From one service to the next, two parts change:

- the service prefix on the action: `s3:`, `sqs:`, `kms:`
- the format of the ARN (Amazon Resource Name, the full ID of an AWS resource) in `Resource`

`Principal` is sometimes there and sometimes not.

## How do a dozen policies sort?

The [IAM policy types page](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies.html) lists 9 policy types: identity-based, resource-based, VPC endpoint policy, permissions boundary, SCP, RCP, ACL, RAM (Resource Access Manager) resource share, session policy.

Eight of them sort with two questions. Is the policy attached to an identity or to a resource? Does it grant access, or only cap it?

| | Grants access | Only caps access |
|---|---|---|
| **Attached to an identity** (no `Principal`) | identity-based policy (including a role's permission policy) | permissions boundary, session policy, SCP |
| **Attached to a resource** (needs `Principal`) | resource-based policy (bucket policy, a role's trust policy, KMS key policy, ..., and the policy a RAM resource share generates) | RCP, VPC endpoint policy |

RAM generates a resource-based policy for you, to share resources like subnets with other accounts, so it counts as resource-based too (see the [RAM managed permissions page](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ram/latest/userguide/security-ram-permissions.html)).

SCP and RCP don't actually attach to an identity or a resource; they attach to an AWS Organizations organization root, OU (organizational unit) or account. The table places them by what they govern:

- An SCP directly limits what the users and roles in the account can do. Its target is already fixed, so it has no `Principal`; the effect is the same as attaching a copy to each identity.
- An RCP limits who can access the resources in the account. A rule written against resources has to say who is accessing them, so an RCP has a `Principal`. It can only be `*`, though; narrowing it takes a `Condition`, for example to deny only accounts outside the organization.

Two exceptions sit outside the table:

- An **ACL** grants access but doesn't use JSON.
- A **CloudFormation stack policy** uses the same JSON but has nothing to do with access, so it isn't one of AWS's 9.

A KMS key policy belongs with "attached to a resource, grants access," but identity-based policies on a KMS key follow one rule that S3 doesn't have; the example is [further down](#kms).

## Question one: attached to an identity, or to a resource?

Say you created a role called `Reader` (an example name, used throughout), and it should be able to read files in the bucket `reports`. There are two places to write that.

### Identity-based policy: on the role

The first place is the role `Reader`. A policy attached to an identity is an identity-based policy (shortened to "identity policy" in the boolean expressions later, and sometimes called an "IAM policy"; all three mean the same thing):

```json
{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": "s3:GetObject",
  "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::reports/*"
}
```

Writing the policy isn't enough; it has to be attached. Save it as `read-reports.json` (wrapped in `"Version"` and `"Statement"`, like the JSON at the top of the article) and attach it to the role:

```
aws iam put-role-policy \
  --role-name Reader \
  --policy-name read-reports \
  --policy-document file://read-reports.json
```

### Resource-based policy: on the bucket

The second place is the bucket `reports`. A policy attached to a resource is a resource-based policy, here a bucket policy. Compared with the one above, it has one extra line:

```diff
 {
   "Effect": "Allow",
+  "Principal": { "AWS": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/Reader" },
   "Action": "s3:GetObject",
   "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::reports/*"
 }
```

### Why only the bucket policy needs a Principal

A bucket policy says who may read the bucket, so `Principal` names them. The one on `Reader` doesn't need it, because the one reading is `Reader` itself. The [IAM Principal element page](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_elements_principal.html) states both rules. Checked in November 2026 with `aws accessanalyzer validate-policy`: the second policy, checked as an identity-based policy, returns `UNSUPPORTED_PRINCIPAL`; the first, checked as a bucket policy, returns `MISSING_PRINCIPAL`.

Every policy listed at the top of the article sits on a resource like this. When unsure, ask: can I attach a policy directly to this thing? If yes, it's resource-based and wants a `Principal`. The "Resource-based policies" column in the [IAM services table](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_aws-services-that-work-with-iam.html) has the full list.

## Which kind is an IAM role's policy?

What people call an "IAM role policy" is really one of two: the permission policy or the trust policy. The first is identity-based, the second resource-based. Both are set in IAM.

Say a Lambda function uses `Reader` to read `reports`.

### Trust policy: who may assume Reader

A trust policy's `Action` depends on how whoever assumes the role signed in (see the [IAM OIDC role page](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_create_for-idp_oidc.html)):

- An AWS user, role or service: `sts:AssumeRole`
- Signed in through OIDC (OpenID Connect), such as GitHub Actions: `sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity`
- Signed in through SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language): `sts:AssumeRoleWithSAML`

This one lets a Lambda assume `Reader`:

```json
{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Principal": { "Service": "lambda.amazonaws.com" },
  "Action": "sts:AssumeRole"
}
```

### Permission policy: what Reader may do once assumed

The permission policy is the one from question one, attached to `Reader` and allowing reads of `reports`.

### How AWS checks the two when the Lambda reads a file

1. The Lambda asks to assume `Reader`.
2. AWS checks the trust policy: `lambda.amazonaws.com` is in `Principal`, so this is allowed.
3. The Lambda gets `Reader`'s temporary credentials.
4. The Lambda calls `s3:GetObject` with them.
5. AWS checks the permission policy: `reports/*` is allowed, so this is allowed.

### Why only the trust policy needs a Principal

A trust policy says who may assume `Reader`, so `Principal` names them. The permission policy doesn't need one, because it sits on `Reader` and the one acting is `Reader` itself. The [IAM services table](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_aws-services-that-work-with-iam.html) calls it the only resource-based policy IAM supports.

A trust policy has no `Resource`, because the resource is the role itself. `validate-policy` rejects a trust policy that includes one with `ROLE_TRUST_POLICY_SYNTAX_ERROR_RESOURCE`.

How trust policies work is covered in [assumeRole and trust policy](/v2/iam-assume-role-trust-policy).

## Question two: does it grant access, or only cap it?

Every policy so far grants access. A few others use the same shape but only set a ceiling and grant nothing themselves. Some attach to identities and some to resources.

### Permissions boundary

A permissions boundary attaches to an IAM user or role and has no `Principal`. Say `Reader`'s identity-based policy allows every S3 action:

```json
{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": "s3:*",
  "Resource": "*"
}
```

`Reader` also has a permissions boundary, `s3-read-only`, that allows only `s3:GetObject`:

```json
{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": "s3:GetObject",
  "Resource": "*"
}
```

Both are the same kind of JSON, attached with different commands:

- Attached with `put-role-policy`, it's an identity-based policy and grants access. If `Reader` has several, they combine with `||`: one allow is enough.
- Attached with `put-role-permissions-boundary` below, it's a permissions boundary and only caps.
- Identity-based policy and permissions boundary combine with `&&`, which the [IAM evaluation page](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_evaluation-logic.html) calls an intersection: `identity-based policy && permissions boundary`.

So `Reader` can do only `s3:GetObject`, which both allow; an `s3:PutObject` call is denied.

The other way round, if the boundary allows `s3:*` and the identity-based policy allows no S3 action, `Reader` has no S3 access.

A boundary has to exist as a managed policy first, then gets attached by its ARN:

```
aws iam create-policy \
  --policy-name s3-read-only \
  --policy-document file://s3-read-only.json

aws iam put-role-permissions-boundary \
  --role-name Reader \
  --permissions-boundary arn:aws:iam::111122223333:policy/s3-read-only
```

### Session policy

A session policy also only caps. It and the trust policy both come up when a role is assumed, so they're easy to mix up. Say the session policy `only-q3.json` allows reading only `reports/q3.pdf`:

```json
{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": "s3:GetObject",
  "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::reports/q3.pdf"
}
```

A caller assumes `Reader` with this command, gets a temporary session, and passes the session policy with `--policy`:

```
aws sts assume-role \
  --role-arn arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/Reader \
  --role-session-name read-q3 \
  --policy file://only-q3.json
```

1. AWS checks `Reader`'s trust policy first. A caller not in its `Principal` can't assume the role.
2. After that, the session can do only what both `Reader`'s permission policy and `only-q3.json` allow.

- `Reader`'s permission policy allows reading all of `reports/*`.
- `only-q3.json` allows reading only `reports/q3.pdf`.
- The session's permissions are `permission policy && session policy`, so it can read only `q3.pdf`.

A session policy isn't attached anywhere; it's passed on each `assume-role` call and affects only that session. The example above has the session policy narrowing access to `q3.pdf`. A session policy can't widen access, though: even if `only-q3.json` were `s3:*`, the session still couldn't do anything `Reader`'s permission policy doesn't allow.

The [IAM policy types page](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies.html) says permissions boundaries and session policies "do not grant permissions." In the expressions `identity-based policy && permissions boundary` and `permission policy && session policy` above, they only appear to the right of `&&`: when the left side is `false`, nothing on the right can make the result `true`.

### SCP

An SCP (service control policy) is an AWS Organizations policy. It attaches to the organization root, an OU or an account, and limits the IAM users and roles underneath. An organization looks roughly like this:

```
organization root
├── management account   ← created the organization, pays the whole organization's bill
├── OU: prod
│   ├── account A
│   └── account B
└── OU: dev
    └── account C
```

Say this SCP is attached to the organization root:

```json
{
  "Effect": "Deny",
  "Action": "s3:DeleteBucket",
  "Resource": "*"
}
```

- A user in account A, B or C who calls `s3:DeleteBucket` is denied, even if their identity-based policy allows `s3:*`.
- The management account is under the root too, but its users and roles can still call `s3:DeleteBucket`. The [SCP page](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_scps.html) says SCPs don't affect users or roles in the management account, or service-linked roles.

Attach the same SCP to `OU: prod` instead, and only accounts A and B are limited.

Because SCPs can't limit the management account, the [Organizations best practices for the management account](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_best-practices_mgmt-acct.html) recommend keeping resources in other accounts. Use the management account only to manage the organization itself, such as creating accounts, creating and attaching SCPs, and viewing the organization's bill.

The same page says that organizations created in the console after July 10, 2026 get an SCP at the root automatically. It denies `organizations:LeaveOrganization` and `account:CloseAccount`, so users and roles in a member account can't take their account out of the organization or close it; those two steps are handled from the management account instead.

An SCP can't have a `Principal`: the [SCP syntax page](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_scps_syntax.html) lists `Principal` and `NotPrincipal` as unsupported.

### RCP

An [RCP](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/introducing-resource-control-policies-rcps-a-new-authorization-policy/) (Resource Control Policy) is an Organizations policy added in November 2024. It attaches to the account that owns the bucket and limits who may access that account's resources. It and an SCP limit different things:

- SCP: what users and roles inside the organization may do.
- RCP: who may access resources in the organization, including accounts outside it.

This one, from the [RCP syntax page](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_rcps_syntax.html), denies any S3 request not made over HTTPS:

```json
{
  "Effect": "Deny",
  "Principal": "*",
  "Action": "s3:*",
  "Resource": "*",
  "Condition": { "BoolIfExists": { "aws:SecureTransport": "false" } }
}
```

An RCP's `Principal` accepts only `*`, and an RCP you write can only use `Deny`. The [RCP syntax page](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_rcps_syntax.html) says `Allow` is supported only in `RCPFullAWSAccess`. When you enable RCPs, AWS attaches that policy to every root, OU and account, and you can't detach it. It lets every request pass the RCP check, so with no `Deny` written, RCPs refuse nothing. An RCP refuses a request only when someone writes a `Deny` and the request matches it. For example, if the bucket policy allows an outside account `s3:GetObject` and an RCP has a `Deny` for accounts outside the organization, that account still can't read the object. Like SCPs, RCPs don't affect resources in the management account (see the [RCP page](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_rcps.html)).

### VPC endpoint policy

A VPC endpoint policy attaches to a VPC endpoint and limits what requests through that endpoint can reach. An endpoint created without a policy gets a default endpoint policy that lets requests through it reach any resource.

One kind of S3 endpoint is the gateway endpoint: EC2 instances in the VPC reach S3 through it without an internet gateway or NAT (see the [S3 gateway endpoint page](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/privatelink/vpc-endpoints-s3.html)). The [VPC endpoint policy page](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/privatelink/vpc-endpoints-access.html) says an endpoint policy must have a `Principal`, and for a gateway endpoint it can only be `*`. Say the endpoint policy on an S3 gateway endpoint is this:

```json
{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Principal": "*",
  "Action": "s3:GetObject",
  "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::reports/*"
}
```

Code in the VPC going through that endpoint can read only `reports`. The endpoint policy only caps; whether `Reader` can read `reports` still comes down to its identity-based policy and the bucket policy.

## What about "deny everyone except X"?

`Principal` has a negated form, `NotPrincipal`. This bucket policy denies everyone except `Admin` access to `reports`:

```json
{
  "Effect": "Deny",
  "NotPrincipal": { "AWS": [
    "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:root",
    "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/Admin"
  ]},
  "Action": "s3:*",
  "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::reports", "arn:aws:s3:::reports/*"]
}
```

`NotPrincipal` still names a who, so for question one it counts the same as `Principal`.

The [IAM NotPrincipal page](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_elements_notprincipal.html) allows `NotPrincipal` only with `Deny`, and never in an identity-based policy or a trust policy. It also recommends against `NotPrincipal` in new policies, in favour of `"Principal": "*"` with an `ArnNotEquals` condition on `aws:PrincipalArn`.

`Action` and `Resource` have negated forms too, `NotAction` and `NotResource`. `"NotAction": "iam:*"` means every action outside IAM (see the [NotAction page](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_elements_notaction.html)).

## Which policies have rules of their own?

<span id="kms"></span>

### KMS key policy

Usually, if `Reader`'s identity-based policy allows `s3:GetObject` and `kms:Decrypt`, it can read KMS-encrypted files (see the [S3 SSE-KMS page](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/UsingKMSEncryption.html)).

That's because the default key policy has a statement whose `Principal` is the account itself (`:root`). Once the key policy allows the account, KMS looks at the account's identity-based policies, and `Reader`'s `kms:Decrypt` counts (see the [KMS default key policy page](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/key-policy-default.html)). If someone writes their own key policy and leaves this statement out, KMS ignores identity-based policies, and `Reader` is denied even with `kms:Decrypt` in its identity-based policy.

The `+` lines below are that statement:

```diff
 {
   "Statement": [
     {
       "Sid": "Allow access for Key Administrators",
       ...
     },
+    {
+      "Sid": "Enable IAM User Permissions",
+      "Effect": "Allow",
+      "Principal": { "AWS": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:root" },
+      "Action": "kms:*",
+      "Resource": "*"
+    }
   ]
 }
```

```
S3:  identity policy || bucket policy
KMS: key policy names Reader || (key policy names :root && identity policy)
```

For S3, the identity-based policy sits inside `||` and is enough on its own; for KMS, it sits to the right of `&&`, so the key policy must allow `:root` first (see the [IAM evaluation page](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_evaluation-logic_policy-eval-denyallow.html)).

### CloudFormation stack policy

A CloudFormation stack policy controls which resources a stack update may change. This one allows every update except deletes (example from the [CloudFormation stack policy page](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/protect-stack-resources.html)):

```json
{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "NotAction": "Update:Delete",
  "Principal": "*",
  "Resource": "*"
}
```

`Principal` is required but accepts only `*`, since there is no "who" to pick. The actions aren't a service's API either; there are three, `Update:Modify`, `Update:Replace` and `Update:Delete`.

## What does `Reader` need to read `reports/q3.pdf`?

For `Reader` reading `q3.pdf` in the same account, the rules on the [IAM policy evaluation page](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_evaluation-logic_policy-eval-denyallow.html) come out as a boolean expression, where any layer that isn't attached counts as `true`:

```
no Deny matches
&& (identity policy 1 || identity policy 2 || bucket policy)
&& permissions boundary
&& session policy
&& SCP && RCP && VPC endpoint policy
&& kms:Decrypt   (if q3.pdf is encrypted with a KMS key)
```

Every `Deny` counts on the first line, whether it sits in the bucket policy, an identity policy or an SCP. The other lines look only at whether that policy has an `Allow`: the `bucket policy` in the parentheses, for example, asks whether the bucket policy has an `Allow` statement that permits this request.

There is no ACL in this expression, because the [IAM policy types page](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies.html) says "ACLs cannot grant permissions to entities within the same account". ACLs can only grant to other accounts and to anonymous requests, so the ACL term appears only in the cross-account expression below.

In the words of the [IAM evaluation page](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_evaluation-logic.html):

- `||` is a union: one allow among the identity-based and resource-based policies is enough.
- `&&` is an intersection: the `||` in parentheses being `true` isn't enough; every other line must be `true` too, including "no Deny matches" on the first line, the caps in the middle, and `kms:Decrypt` on the last.

Across accounts, the expression changes. Say `Reader` is in account A and `reports` in account B:

```
same account:   identity policy 1 || identity policy 2 || bucket policy
cross-account:  (identity policy 1 || identity policy 2) && (bucket policy || ACL)
```

- Same account: one allow among the three is enough.
- Cross-account: accounts A and B each check their own side, and both must allow it (see the [IAM cross-account evaluation page](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_evaluation-logic-cross-account.html)).
  - Account A checks the policies on `Reader`: is `Reader` allowed to read someone else's bucket? `identity policy 1 || identity policy 2`, one allow is enough.
  - Account B checks the policies on `reports`: does `reports` let account A's `Reader` in? `bucket policy || ACL`, one allow is enough.
  - The two groups are joined by `&&`: only when A says yes and B says yes can `Reader` read the file.

Applied to concrete setups. In these examples `Reader` and `reports` are in the same account, except in the cross-account row:

| Setup | Readable? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Identity-based policy allows `s3:*`; bucket policy also lets in `Reader`; nothing else | ✅ | all = `true` |
| Only the identity-based policy allows it; bucket policy doesn't mention `Reader` | ✅ | `identity policy` = `true`, so `\|\|` = `true` |
| Identity-based policy silent; bucket policy names `Reader`'s role ARN | ✅ | `bucket policy` = `true`, so `\|\|` = `true` |
| `Reader` in another account; only the identity-based policy allows it | ❌ | `(bucket policy \|\| ACL)` = `false` |
| Identity-based policy allows `s3:*`; bucket policy has a `Deny` naming `Reader` | ❌ | a `Deny` matches, so denied |
| Identity-based and bucket policies allow it; the SCP on `Reader`'s account denies `s3:GetObject` | ❌ | a `Deny` matches, so denied |
| Identity-based policy allows `s3:*`; permissions boundary allows only `s3:ListBucket` | ❌ | `permissions boundary` = `false` |
| Request goes through a VPC endpoint whose policy allows only another bucket | ❌ | `VPC endpoint policy` = `false` |
| All S3 permissions allow it, but `q3.pdf` is KMS-encrypted and the key policy lacks the `:root` statement | ❌ | `kms:Decrypt` = `false` (see [KMS key policy](#kms)) |

ACL and Block Public Access settings are covered in the next two subsections, and can be flipped in the embed in the Block Public Access one.

### With ACLs on, an Allow-only bucket policy is undone however precise it is

Besides policies, S3 has an older access system, the **ACL** (access control list): the `ACL` in `bucket policy || ACL` in the cross-account expression above; anonymous requests are checked against it too. The [IAM policy types page](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies.html) calls ACLs the only policy type that doesn't use JSON.

Say the bucket policy on `reports` lets in only `Reader`, and ACLs are still enabled. Someone uploads `q3.pdf` with `--acl public-read`:

```
aws s3 cp q3.pdf s3://reports/ --acl public-read
```

1. `q3.pdf`'s ACL gains a grant: `AllUsers` may `READ`.
2. The bucket policy still names only `Reader`.
3. Anyone can GET the file's URL, unsigned, and read it.

The grant looks like this. No `Effect`, no `Action`, no `Condition`:

```xml
<Grant>
  <Grantee xsi:type="Group">
    <URI>http://acs.amazonaws.com/groups/global/AllUsers</URI>
  </Grantee>
  <Permission>READ</Permission>
</Grant>
```

The [S3 ACL page](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/acl-overview.html) says `AllUsers` means anyone, signed or anonymous. An anonymous request has no identity policy, so only the `reports` side counts: `bucket policy || ACL`. The bucket policy doesn't name it, but the `ACL` term is `true`, so the `||` holds. If the bucket policy has only `Allow` statements, however strict, `q3.pdf` is public. Add the `Deny` below to the bucket policy, though, and the first line, "no Deny matches", fails, so the ACL grant doesn't help. The [IAM policy variables page](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_variables.html) says an anonymous request's `aws:PrincipalType` is `Anonymous`, so this denies only anonymous requests and leaves `Reader` alone:

```json
{
  "Effect": "Deny",
  "Principal": "*",
  "Action": "s3:GetObject",
  "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::reports/*",
  "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "aws:PrincipalType": "Anonymous" } }
}
```

### Block Public Access: do public ACLs and bucket policies count?

The left side of the embed below holds the switches: Object Ownership (a three-way choice, one option of which disables ACLs), the four Block Public Access switches, and how `q3.pdf` was encrypted when uploaded, with the KMS key policy below that. The right side holds the bucket policy JSON and `q3.pdf`'s object ACL. Statements can be added to or removed from the bucket policy and the KMS key policy; the KMS key policy's statements appear after you open "2 statements". The object ACL is shown as is.

- Set Object Ownership to Bucket owner enforced, which disables ACLs, and `q3.pdf`'s object ACL and the `BlockPublicAcls` and `IgnorePublicAcls` switches turn grey, because S3 no longer counts ACLs when checking access.
- The four lines at the top right are the results. Their text never changes; only the colour gives the answer: normal ink means yes, faded means no.

<iframe src="/embeds/s3-access-tree" width="100%" height="1084" style="border:0;display:block;margin:1.5rem 0 2.5rem" loading="lazy" title="S3 bucket settings tree: what decides whether q3.pdf can be read"></iframe>

Block Public Access isn't a single switch but a set of four. Each can be on or off on its own; the [S3 Block Public Access page](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/access-control-block-public-access.html) says "These settings are independent and can be used in any combination." They deal with *public* ACLs and bucket policies. A public ACL is a grant to `AllUsers` like the one above; a public bucket policy is one like the `Principal: "*"` statement in the embed, with no limiting `Condition`, so anyone can read.

In the console's wording, two of the four act on *new* ones and two on *any*:

- `BlockPublicAcls`, `BlockPublicPolicy` (*new*): S3 rejects any attempt to write a public ACL or bucket policy. Existing ones are untouched; `q3.pdf`'s ACL stays in force.
- `IgnorePublicAcls`, `RestrictPublicBuckets` (*any*): existing ones aren't deleted, but stop working for outsiders. A public ACL doesn't count, so anonymous requests can't read `q3.pdf`; a public bucket policy works only for users in the bucket owner's account and AWS services. `Reader` still reads through policies in its own account.

If the account, organization or an access point also sets these switches, S3 compares them one switch at a time: a switch on in any of those places counts as on for `reports`. If the account has `IgnorePublicAcls` on, public ACLs in `reports` don't count even though the bucket itself has it off. The organization is the exception: the [Block Public Access page](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/access-control-block-public-access.html) says that at the organization level all four settings apply together, and you can't turn on just one.

### The 2023 defaults

[Since April 2023](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/heads-up-amazon-s3-security-changes-are-coming-in-april-of-2023/), new buckets have all four on and [ACLs disabled](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/about-object-ownership.html) ("Bucket owner enforced"). With ACLs disabled:

- the `--acl public-read` upload above fails with a 400 `AccessControlListNotSupported`;
- existing ACLs no longer take part in access evaluation; the `ACL` term in the expression is never true, and only the policies decide.

## The takeaway

Next time AWS hands you a new "X policy," ask two questions:

1. **Does it name a who, with `Principal` or `NotPrincipal`?** If yes, it sits on a resource; if no, on an identity. SCP and RCP are the exception: they attach to an Organizations root, OU or account.
2. **Does it grant access, or only cap it?** If the docs say it does "not grant permissions," it only caps.

Then find its cell in the table above. For a KMS key, the key policy must first allow the key's account to use identity-based policies before any identity-based policy takes effect.
